status2026.detail: The APS Beamline Directory entry for 19-ID-E, fetched on 9 October 2026, lists ISN as 'Operational/Accepting General Users' with access via on-site beamline staff. The path there: technical commissioning of the endstation and KB optics in summer 2025. Stage 4, technical commissioning, on the 24 Nov 2025 APS progress graphic. Stage 5, scientific commissioning and early experiments, on the 26 Jan 2026 graphic. The Aug 2025 APS-U update had forecast first experiments 'either late this year or early next year' and general users 'either late in the first run of 2026 or sometime in the second run'. A 31 Jul 2026 Argonne job posting still describes duties as 'commissioning and operation of the ISN'. So 2026 is best read as early user operations with some commissioning still going on. The design target is a 20 nm spot at 25 keV. Abstracts from late 2025 and 2026 quote ~25–30 nm. For context, the APS Upgrade project as a whole was formally completed in early 2026, and Argonne's Sept 2026 nanoscience feature presents ISN as a powerful new in situ tool.

tagline: A 220-metre X-ray microscope that watches batteries, catalysts and solar cells at work, in spots just tens of nanometres wide.
summary: The In Situ Nanoprobe (ISN) is an X-ray microscope built to watch materials while they work: a battery charging, a catalyst in hot gas, a solar-cell film being baked into shape. It squeezes X-rays into a spot designed to be 20 nanometres across, about 4,500 times thinner than a hair (first measurements report 25–30 nm), and scans the sample through it. At every point it records which elements fluoresce, how the atoms are stacked, what current or light the X-rays spark, and a diffraction pattern that a computer turns into an even sharper image. The challenge is space: heaters and gas or liquid cells need 5–6 cm in front of the sample, so the focusing mirrors must be long and lit by coherent light. That is why the beamline runs about 220 m, out of the ring building to a vibration-isolated concrete room where the air holds to ±0.05 °C over an hour.

whatAPSUEnables.text: A nanoprobe can make its smallest spot only from the coherent part of an X-ray beam, the part whose waves stay in step across the beam; the rest is thrown away at a pair of tiny slits that act as a clean secondary source. The old APS electron beam was about 275 µm wide (root-mean-square width), so little of its light was coherent; the design's brightness mode squeezes it to about 15 µm and cuts its emittance (beam size × angular spread) roughly 70-fold. ISN's layout depends on this: a 220 m beamline whose long mirrors focus 61 mm past their ends, upstream wobbles filtered out by the slits, and enough coherent flux at 20–30 keV to pass through cell windows, water and gas. The 2017 design estimated 1,000 to 10,000 times more focused flux than pre-upgrade nanoprobes for spectroscopy, and 10,000 to 100,000 times for mapping with the wide-band multilayer monochromator, whose installation is unconfirmed. No measured focused flux has been published yet.
quantitative: The electron beam shrinks from ~275 µm (H) × 10 µm (V) before the upgrade to ~15 × 4 µm in brightness mode; brightness rises up to 500×.

Horizontal source size is reduced ~20× (FDR sec. 4-7.1). A horizontal emittance below 30 pm·rad has been measured by grating interferometry at 3-ID-B; from the pre-upgrade ring to APS-U the emittance falls ~70-fold.
Coherent flux after the BDAs: 7.2 × 10¹² ph/s at 10 keV (coherent fraction 5.58%) and 4.7 × 10¹¹ ph/s at 25 keV (0.94%) (FDR Table 4.51).
Design focused flux at 25 keV: 3.4 × 10¹¹ ph/s coherent into 16 × 16 nm² FWHM, or 3.1 × 10¹² ph/s into 24 × 30 nm² with the BDAs open (FDR Table 4.52).
Design focused flux at 10 keV: 3.5 × 10¹² ph/s coherent into 39 × 39 nm², or 8.9 × 10¹² ph/s into 43 × 52 nm² (FDR Table 4.52).

The JACoW abstract of the MEDSI'25 paper quotes a focused flux above 3 × 10¹¹ ph/s at 25 keV. This restates the design capability (cf. FDR 3.4 × 10¹¹ ph/s coherent); the paper itself reports no measured flux.

2017 design estimate: a focused-flux gain of 10³–10⁴ over pre-upgrade nanoprobes for spectroscopy (0.01% bandwidth), and 10⁴–10⁵ for elemental mapping and ptychography (1% bandwidth, i.e. with the multilayer monochromator).

KB mirrors vs diffractive optics: ~10× higher focusing efficiency at 10 keV and ~100× at 30 keV. The DMM with the achromatic KB pair gives ~25× more flux than the DCM where chemical-state contrast is not needed.
Expected reduction in acquisition time: a factor of 100 or more.

techniques.name: Scanning X-ray fluorescence microscopy and fluorescence tomography
techniques.text: When the focused X-ray spot knocks an inner electron out of an atom, the atom refills the gap and emits a fluorescence X-ray whose energy is a fingerprint of the element. Scanning the spot across the sample builds a map of where each element sits, down to trace amounts; rotating the sample and repeating turns the maps into 3D (fluorescence tomography). ISN reads the fluorescence with silicon-drift detectors, a 7-element unit or a 12-element backscatter unit, and scans on the fly at up to 1 mm/s over a 10 × 10 mm area. Because mirrors focus all energies alike, the broad 1% band of the designed multilayer monochromator could speed up mapping, and recovering the exact shape of the X-ray spot by ptychography, a coherent-imaging method, lets the maps be sharpened to about 10 nm.

techniques.name: XRF nanospectroscopy (nano-XANES spectromicroscopy)
techniques.text: Stepping the X-ray energy across an element's absorption edge, the energy at which its inner electrons can just be knocked loose, reveals its chemical state, for example rusted versus metallic iron. This is X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) spectroscopy, read here through the fluorescence in a spot only tens of nanometres wide, so it can tell the chemistry of one tiny particle from its neighbour. The liquid-nitrogen-cooled Si(111) crystal monochromator sets the energy to 1.4 parts in 10,000, and because the mirror focus does not depend on energy, the spot stays on the same point during a scan; only the undulator gap and crystal angle track the energy. The 4.8–30 keV range covers the K edges (of the innermost electron shell) from titanium (4.97 keV) to tin (29.20 keV), plus the L₃ edges (of the next shell) of the rare earths and of heavy elements such as lead and bismuth.

techniques.name: Ptychography (2D and 3D coherent diffractive imaging)
techniques.text: Instead of only counting X-rays, a camera far behind the sample records the diffraction pattern made at each of many overlapping spot positions. A computer works backward from thousands of these patterns to an image sharper than the spot itself; the design goal was below 10 nm for samples thin enough to let X-rays through. ISN's diffraction-limited focus is inherently coherent, which this method needs, so ptychography can run alongside fluorescence mapping. The camera rides a table with 6 m of travel along the beam and also records small-angle scattering and absorption. Planned data rates are about 5 GB/s, part of roughly 10 PB of raw data a year across ISN, processed on Argonne's Aurora supercomputer; the method also recovers the shape of the X-ray probe, a useful check on the mirrors.

techniques.name: Nano-diffraction / X-ray diffraction microscopy
techniques.text: Crystals diffract X-rays into bright spots at angles set by the spacing of their atomic planes. An industrial robot arm carries a camera around the sample to catch these spots, revealing which crystal phase is present at each point and how it changes as the sample is heated or charged. The diffracted X-rays leave the sample chamber through a 0.5 mm beryllium dome window, tipped 10° up and 25° outboard (away from the ring), that passes a cone of about 0.25 steradian. At ISN, diffraction is an auxiliary contrast for following phase changes during in situ work, alongside fluorescence.

techniques.name: X-ray beam induced current / voltage
techniques.text: In a solar cell or LED, the X-ray spot frees charge carriers much as light does when the device is working. Measuring the resulting current (X-ray beam-induced current, XBIC) or voltage (XBIV) at each point of the scan shows which nanoscale regions collect charge well and which defects kill performance. ISN reads it with a sensitive four-channel picoammeter, pixel by pixel together with the fluorescence map, so composition and defects can be compared directly with local charge collection.

techniques.name: X-ray excited optical luminescence microscopy
techniques.text: Some materials glow with visible or infrared light when X-rays hit them, an effect called X-ray excited optical luminescence (XEOL). ISN has a built-in vacuum light microscope just upstream of the sample that collects this glow through a fold mirror with a hole for the X-rays, so emission from, for example, a perovskite or LED material can be linked to the chemistry at the same spot. It sees a 600 µm field with 1 µm resolution and sends light from 430 to 1,800 nm to a fibre-coupled spectrometer; an external module can also shine excitation or bias light onto the sample.

scienceCases.title: Watching a solar-cell absorber form
scienceCases.text: Thin-film solar cells such as CIGS (copper indium gallium selenide) are cooked at about 600 °C in selenium- or sulfur-bearing gas, and tiny defects that form along the way can ruin efficiency. ISN is designed to follow where copper, indium, gallium and selenium move while the film forms, comparing fluorescence, beam-induced current and luminescence point by point. A pre-upgrade demonstration at 600 °C needed about 7 minutes per 10 × 10 µm map; ISN aims to cut map times more than 100-fold, with doses low enough for beam-sensitive halide perovskites.

scienceCases.title: Battery particles, one crystallite at a time
scienceCases.text: Battery electrodes are powders of tiny crystals; some take up lithium faster than others, and some crack or degrade. In olivine cathodes such as lithium manganese iron phosphate (LMFP) the individual crystallites are only 25–200 nm across, so fast chemical mapping by nano-XANES (X-ray absorption near-edge structure spectroscopy) with a 20 nm beam, helped by diffraction, can resolve mixed phases inside one crystallite while the battery cycles. The as-built electrochemical holder has two fluid inlets, heats above 100 °C, takes bulk electrodes and a flow cell more than 200 µm thick, and rotates for tomography.

scienceCases.title: Catalysts caught in the act
scienceCases.text: Most fuels and chemicals are made with catalysts, and catalysts change shape and chemistry once they are taken out of the reactor. ISN's gas cell heats samples to 1,000 °C in flowing gas, with two pressure-controlled gas inlets and four electrical bias channels, so the active metals can be seen as they work. Design studies target metal poisoning by iron and nickel in fluid-catalytic-cracking particles, the chemical state near grain boundaries of copper electrocatalysts for CO₂ reduction under bias, and buried interfaces in photo-electrochemical devices.

scienceCases.title: Finding stray atoms in next-generation chips
scienceCases.text: Modern transistors are only a few nanometres wide, and a few misplaced metal atoms can make the insulation between them fail. ISN's hard X-rays pass through a whole intact chip, so it can look for dopants, impurities and defects in stacked 3D devices, for example in high-k dielectrics (the high-permittivity insulating layers) and in copper or cobalt wiring at the 7 nm technology node and beyond. The 2017 science case describes ISN as the only non-destructive tool sensitive to impurities at 0.1% or below in small regions of an intact system.

scienceCases.title: Electrochemical interfaces for fuel cells and electrolyzers
scienceCases.text: Fuel cells and water electrolysers rely on thin layers of precious metals whose structure shifts as they run. Proposals from the 2023 first-experiments workshop for ISN and its sister nanoprobe PtychoProbe include mapping the functional phases in fuel-cell and electrolyser electrodes while they are made and run, following partial gold and platinum films on iridium crystals over 10–100 nm in liquid, where surface diffusion is faster than in gas, and vacancy formation in atomically thin catalysts for hydrogen evolution. The gold and platinum study names a purpose-built electrochemical cell as the key enabler, which is where ISN's long working distance matters. These are proposals, not yet results.

scienceCases.title: Environmental and quantum materials
scienceCases.text: The same tool can look for valuable metals and toxic elements in coal ash, follow microbes at soil and gas interfaces, or study carbon stored underground. For quantum materials, an APS-built holder cooled by a closed-cycle helium cryostat reaches 40 K (−233 °C) and goes up to 355 K, designed for ultralow vibration; it was still in development when last described. Workshop topics also include growing epitaxial complex-oxide films in situ and driving quantum materials out of equilibrium.

insertionDevices.name: APS21R25#1 (upstream revolver undulator)
insertionDevices.type: planar hybrid permanent-magnet revolver undulator (two magnet structures on a rotating strongback)
insertionDevices.notes: Selectable structures: APS21#6, 2.1 cm × 112 periods (Keff 1.38, E1 8.35 keV at 8.5 mm), or APS25#5, 2.5 cm × 94 periods (Keff 2.00, E1 4.56 keV). Length is estimate from N × period (2.35 m), consistent with the nominal 2.4 m inline devices. Gap specs: 8.5 mm minimum gap, 5 mm maximum taper, revolve only with the gap open. U25 covers the 4.8 keV low end continuously. U21 boosts brilliance at high energy.

insertionDevices.name: APS21R25#2 (downstream revolver undulator)
insertionDevices.notes: Selectable structures: APS21#7, 2.1 cm × 112 periods, or APS25#2, 2.5 cm × 94 periods. The listed 25 mm period represents one selectable structure; either can be active. FDR Table 3.13 lists a phase shifter/corrector between the two in-line devices to keep them in phase.

source.canting: none (dual in-line, not canted; phase shifter/corrector between devices per FDR Table 3.13)
source.frontEnd: Standard APS-U high-heat-load front end (HHLFE), based on the 28-ID design. Rated 21 kW total and 590 kW/mrad² peak. Windowless exit via a differential pumping section. Components: clearing magnet, burn-through fixed mask, fixed masks, photon shutter with intensity monitor IM1, GRID XBPM1, safety shutters, and an exit mask with XBPM2. ISN exit mask: 2 × 2 mm² at 25.4 m, then a 5 × 5 mm² exit collimator at 26.1 m. Up to 2.28 kW passes the mask.
source.sourceSizeAndDivergence: Nominal APS-U ID electron-beam source at zero current. Flat-beam mode (κ=0.1): σx = 14.5 µm, σx' = 2.75 µrad, σy = 3.1 µm, σy' = 1.29 µrad. Round-beam mode: σx = 12.3 µm, σx' = 2.34 µrad, σy = 8.3 µm, σy' = 3.47 µrad. Single-electron photon contribution at 25 keV for L ≈ 4.7 m (computed, σr = √(2λL)/4π, σr' = √(λ/2L)): ≈1.7 µm and ≈2.3 µrad. Which mode a given run uses changes the vertical source size and therefore the BDA-V settings.

branches.name: ISN nanoprobe line (single branch)
branches.description: One monochromatic branch: two revolver undulators → windowless HHL front end → 19-ID-A (M1, M2, DCM/DMM, M3) → 19-ID-C (BDA-V at 55 m) → 19-ID-D (BDA-H at 64 m, shutter) → ~147 m transport → 19-ID-E in the Long Beamline Building (KB nanofocus at 220 m, beamstop at 227 m). The instrument is fixed in location and runs only in fixed-exit, KB-focused monochromatic mode (FDR 4-7.7.4).

components.name: Upstream revolver undulator (APS21R25#1)
components.distanceNote: Approximate: two ~2.35 m devices (N × period) and a short phase shifter share the ~4.8 m straight; centres drawn 1.25 m either side of the straight-section centre (source point = 0). Exact centres are not published.
components.text: The upstream of two undulators in the ring's straight section: a 2.35 m row of alternating permanent magnets that makes the passing 6 GeV electrons wiggle, so they emit a bright, narrow X-ray beam. Like a revolver, it carries two magnet rows on one rotating support and turns, with its gap open, to swap between them: the 25 mm-period row reaches down to 4.56 keV and covers ISN's low-energy end, while the 21 mm row (lowest fundamental energy 8.35 keV) boosts brightness at high energy. At the 8.5 mm minimum gap and 200 mA it radiates 5.4 kW (21 mm) or 8.1 kW (25 mm); users work at 8.7 mm or more.

components.name: Phase shifter / corrector
components.distanceNote: Approximate: between the two in-line undulators at the straight-section centre (inferred from FDR Table 3.13).
components.text: A short magnet between the two undulators that delays the electrons by a hair, so the light from both devices adds up in step instead of partly cancelling. The right delay changes with the undulator gap, so it must be adjustable. The design lists a phase shifter/corrector here, but its as-built form is not confirmed in public sources.

components.name: Downstream revolver undulator (APS21R25#2)
components.distanceNote: Approximate (see the upstream device): centre ~1.25 m downstream of the straight-section centre.
components.text: The second revolver undulator, built like the first and placed directly behind it. Lined up and kept in step by the phase shifter, the pair acts like one undulator about 4.7 m long and makes the beam roughly twice as bright as one device alone.

components.name: High-heat-load front end (HHLFE)
components.distanceNote: Schematic placeholder: the front end runs inside the storage-ring tunnel from roughly 14 m to the FOE at ~24–26 m. No 19-ID-specific positions are published apart from the exit mask and collimator. The windowless exit uses a differential pumping section, placed at ~25.5 m in the 2017 PDR layout.
components.text: The front end, inside the thick concrete shielding of the accelerator tunnel, stands guard between the ring and the beamline: masks absorb unwanted power, shutters can stop the beam, and position monitors check where it points. It is the standard high-heat-load design of the upgraded APS, rated for 21 kW in total and 590 kW/mrad² at the beam's centre. ISN's has no exit window, only a differential pumping section that keeps the vacuums apart, so nothing disturbs the beam's wavefront.

components.name: Front-end exit mask (with XBPM2)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49.
components.text: A thick metal block with a 2 mm square hole, the last aperture of the front end. Only the bright core of the undulator's X-ray fan gets through, still carrying up to 2.28 kW, and a built-in position monitor checks where the beam points. A 2020 shielding study assumed a 2 mm wide × 1 mm tall opening; the as-built value is not confirmed.

components.name: Front-end exit collimator
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49.
components.text: A heavy-metal block with a 5 mm square opening that stops bremsstrahlung (high-energy gamma rays made when stored electrons strike leftover gas in the ring) while letting the X-ray beam through. For the upgrade its opening was narrowed to 5 × 5 mm², so beamlines whose monochromators shift the beam only slightly sideways can still keep the bremsstrahlung contained.

components.name: White-beam slits (19ID-SL-1)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49. A small pump stand (RGA, gauges) sits at 27.3 m.
components.text: Four adjustable jaws that trim the raw white beam, which still holds every X-ray energy the undulators emit. Their opening sets how much of the first mirror is lit and how much heat it must absorb.

components.name: M1 flat high-heat-load mirror (19ID-MR-1)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49 (Knopp 2018 also gives 28 m). M1 and M2 share one vacuum vessel in the FOE drawing (NIMA 2020 Fig. 3a).
components.text: A flat, water-cooled silicon mirror 40 cm long that the beam skims at 2.5 mrad, about a seventh of a degree, reflecting it downward. Its three stripes (bare silicon, chromium and platinum) each reflect only up to a certain energy, so choosing one rejects unwanted high-energy harmonics across 4.8–30 keV. It absorbs up to 455 W; a side notch with cooling above it cuts heat-induced bending about tenfold. Together with M2 it lowers the beam by about 5 mm.

components.name: M2 bendable vertical focusing mirror (19ID-MR-2)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49.
components.text: A second mirror, facing up, that tips the beam back to level. Bent by a whisker into a gentle curve, it also focuses the beam vertically onto a tiny slit 26 m downstream, nearly one-to-one, and the bend corrects heat bumps on both mirrors. It sees only the pink beam, which still spans a broad band of energies, and absorbs about 13 W. Sources disagree on the tightest bend needed: about 10 km in the 2019 final design, but 4.38 km at 5 keV in a 2018 heat-load study.

components.name: Secondary bremsstrahlung collimator (19ID-SC-1)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49 (listed at 29.7 m together with PM-1).
components.text: A lead shielding block that stops stray radiation travelling along the old straight-through path, which the mirrored beam no longer uses. It sits just after the mirror pair, together with the white-beam stop.

components.name: Photon mask / white-beam stop (19ID-PM-1)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49.
components.text: A stop that catches any raw white beam that missed the mirrors. Only the mirror-reflected pink beam, already stripped of its highest energies and now about 5 mm lower, slips past underneath; the 5 mm is a geometric estimate (5 mrad × 1.0 m between the mirrors).

components.name: Diagnostic flag (19ID-BD-1)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49.
components.text: A pop-in fluorescent screen. It glows where the X-rays hit, so staff can watch the beam on a camera and line it up after the mirrors.

components.name: Pink-beam slits (19ID-SL-2)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49.
components.text: Adjustable jaws that limit the size of the pink beam, and so the heat, reaching the monochromators. Like the white-beam slits, they are built for high heat loads.

components.name: Double-crystal monochromator, LN₂-cooled H-DCM (19ID-MN-1)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49 (FOE drawing places it at ~31.4 m).
components.text: The monochromator: two perfect silicon crystals, cooled with liquid nitrogen, that pass a single X-ray energy with a spread of only 1.4 parts in 10,000. Turning them sweeps the energy across an element's absorption edge to read its chemical state, while the exit beam stays fixed. They bounce the beam sideways rather than up or down, so any distortion they add stays out of the vertical, where the source is smallest and most coherent. The price is polarization: the undulator light is polarized horizontally, so a sideways reflection is less efficient; the 2017 preliminary design puts the reflectivity at about 83% at 5 keV.

components.name: Double-multilayer monochromator (19ID-MN-2)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49 (FOE drawing places it at ~32.5 m). As-built status unconfirmed: the beamline directory lists only the H-DCM.
components.text: A wide-band alternative to the crystals: two mirrors coated with 300 pairs of alternating nanometre-thin layers of molybdenum and boron carbide, which reflect a band of energies about 1% wide instead of the crystals' 0.014%. Where chemical detail is not needed, that gives roughly 25 times more X-rays for fast element maps. It is in the design, but the 2026 beamline directory lists only the crystal monochromator, so whether it has been installed is not confirmed.

specs.conservative alternative: d = 2.0 nm, 600 bilayers (40% narrower band, 15% lower reflectance)

components.name: Pink-beam missteering mask (19ID-PM-2)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49.
components.text: A safety mask that catches the pink beam if it is ever steered the wrong way, so it cannot strike unprotected parts of the beamline.

components.name: Primary bremsstrahlung collimator (19ID-BC-1)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49.
components.text: A lead collimator that keeps the most energetic stray radiation, the bremsstrahlung gamma rays from the accelerator, inside this first optics enclosure. It is the primary collimator, the main barrier between the straight-through radiation and the hutches downstream.

components.name: Pink-beam slits (19ID-SL-3)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49.
components.text: Adjustable jaws just before M3 that set how much of the horizontal focusing mirror the beam lights up, and so how much of the beam reaches the horizontal slit at 64 m.

components.name: M3 horizontal focusing mirror (19ID-MR-3)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49; the NIMA 2020 FOE drawing shows M3 at the downstream end of 19-ID-A. NOTE: FDR Fig. 4.40 (and the 2017 PDR) label this mirror at 43 m, which is superseded.
components.text: A platinum-coated mirror that turns the beam 5 mrad (about 0.3°) toward the ring and, gently bent, focuses it side to side onto the second tiny slit, 29 m downstream. From here on the whole beamline follows this slightly turned line, which ends roughly 0.9 m inboard of the straight-through path at 220 m. It accepts beam from either monochromator. The 2017 preliminary design put this mirror at 43 m, where it would have shrunk the source image by half; at 35 m, its position in the final design, it images the source almost one-to-one (0.83×, a geometric estimate).

components.name: Shielded transport 19-ID-A to 19-ID-C (19ID-ST-1)
components.distanceNote: Exact span 35.8–48.2 m (FDR Table 4.49); midpoint given. The FDR table says 'to 19-ID-B', but the FDR's own optics text places BDA-V 'in enclosure C' and the NIMA 2020 plan labels the hutch 19-ID-C, so 'B' looks like a table error.
components.text: A lead-shielded vacuum pipe, 12.4 m long, that carries the beam across the open experiment-hall floor from the first optics enclosure to the first aperture hutch, 19-ID-C. Outside the hutches, this shielding is what keeps the hall safe for people walking past.

components.name: Missteering mask and bremsstrahlung collimator/stop (19ID-PM-3, 19ID-BC-2)
components.distanceNote: Exact: PM-3 at 49.1 m, BC-2 at 49.5 m (FDR Table 4.49); one hotspot at 49.3 m.
components.text: Safety blocks at the entrance of the first aperture hutch: a mask that catches a mis-steered pink beam, and a lead collimator and stop against stray radiation from the accelerator.

components.name: Vertical beam-defining aperture, BDA-V (19ID-SL-4)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49; consistent with the NIMA 2020 plan (scaled).
components.text: The heart of ISN's design. M2 focuses the beam onto this slit, which can close to about 3.5–4 µm, roughly half the width of a red blood cell, and what passes becomes a small, clean, steady secondary source for the final mirrors 165 m away. Because those mirrors see only this source, wobbles and wavefront errors of the optics upstream are filtered out. Closed to about 4 µm, the design setting for a fully coherent focus at 25 keV, it gives the sharpest spot; opened, it passes more X-rays into a slightly larger spot. Its jaws take the beam at a grazing angle: with the multilayer monochromator up to 11.6 W can land on them, enough to heat a head-on slit past 850 K.

components.name: Horizontal beam-defining aperture, BDA-H (19ID-SL-5)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49; consistent with the NIMA 2020 plan (scaled).
components.text: The matching side-to-side slit, at the focus of M3. Together the two slits act as a tiny adjustable pinhole that turns the large, slightly wobbly beam into a small, steady source, so vibrations in the optics upstream do not reach the sample. For a fully coherent 16 nm focus at 25 keV the design sets the pair to 13.0 µm wide and 4.1 µm tall. The horizontal slit can be the wider one because the short horizontal mirror accepts only a narrow slice of the beam, and light from a wider slit is still coherent across that slice.

components.name: Photon shutter (19ID-SH-1)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49.
components.text: A heavy, water-cooled safety shutter. It closes so people can enter the distant endstation while the optics upstream keep running. It is rated for pink beam because, with the monochromator retracted, a mirror-reflected beam could travel down the long transport.

components.name: Long shielded mono-beam transport (19ID-ST-2)
components.distanceNote: Exact span 65.5–213.0 m (FDR Table 4.49); midpoint given. Shielded ion-pump stations at 95, 124, 153 and 183 m.
components.enclosure: Experiment hall, LOM area and enclosed corridor to the Long Beamline Building
components.text: About 147 m of 4-inch (about 10 cm) vacuum pipe in lead shielding, longer than one and a half football fields. It carries the beam out of the experiment hall, through part of the laboratory and office wing and an enclosed corridor, to ISN's endstation in the Long Beamline Building. Ion pumps in shielded stations every 29 m or so keep the pressure near 2 × 10⁻⁷ mbar at the pumps and 1 × 10⁻⁶ mbar between them, according to the design model. The pipe is wide enough that a mirror-only beam could reach the endstation, so the endstation is shielded for that case.

components.name: Double Si₃N₄ exit window (19ID-WN-1)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49.
components.text: Two ultra-thin silicon-nitride windows that seal the beamline's vacuum off from the endstation. ISN keeps windows to the very end, and its front end has none at all, because every window slightly disturbs the beam's coherent wavefront.

components.name: Attenuator / filter box (19ID-FL-1)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49.
components.text: Thin foils that can slide into the beam to dim it for delicate samples. They belong to the endstation's beam-conditioning section, which sits on granite blocks, mostly in low vacuum.

components.name: Beam-conditioning section: scintillator BPMs, clean-up slits, PIN diodes
components.distanceNote: Approximate: between the window (213.0 m) and the KB optics (~219.6 m), on granite blocks (MEDSI'25 Fig. 3). No individual positions published.
components.text: Cameras, sensors and clean-up slits on heavy granite blocks, the last checks before the microscope. Two scintillator screens act as beam-position monitors, two PIN diodes (silicon photodiodes) measure how many X-rays arrive, and the slits trim away stray light. The granite gives the stability these checks need.

components.name: Fast shutter (19ID-FS-1)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49.
components.text: A quick-acting shutter that lets X-rays onto the sample only while data are being taken, to limit radiation damage. It sits in the endstation's beam-conditioning line, ahead of the focusing mirrors.

components.name: Vertical nanofocusing KB mirror (KBV)
components.distanceNote: Derived: q_v = 396 mm upstream of the 220.0 m focus (MEDSI'25 Fig. 5a); p = 165.004 m from BDA-V at 55 m.
components.text: The first of the two final focusing mirrors, in the Kirkpatrick–Baez (KB) arrangement, where one curved mirror focuses vertically and the next horizontally. This one is 404 mm of silicon shaped to within 2 nm of a perfect ellipse; skimming the beam at 2.5 mrad, it takes in about 1 mm of beam and brings it to a focus 396 mm downstream, an image of the slit 165 m upstream shrunk about 400-fold. To keep a ~20 nm spot still, its tilt must hold to 5 nanoradians. During commissioning it held 0.4 nrad rms (root-mean-square), a preliminary figure measured in air with the vacuum pumps off.

specs.stability: 5 nrad required; preliminary 0.4 nrad rms measurement in air with vacuum pumps off

components.name: Horizontal nanofocusing KB mirror (KBH)
components.distanceNote: Derived: q_h = 125.5 mm upstream of the 220.0 m focus (MEDSI'25 Fig. 5a).
components.text: The second, shorter Kirkpatrick–Baez mirror, 129 mm long, focuses the beam side to side. Its end stops 61 mm before the focus, leaving room for heaters, gas cells and liquid cells around the sample; in practice the chamber walls leave less, about 47–55 mm. That working distance is the reason for ISN's long mirrors and 220 m length. Its angle must hold to 16 nanoradians, a looser limit than the vertical mirror's 5 nrad because it sits closer to the focus. It hangs from a gantry so the sample chamber fits underneath.

specs.usable space: 47 mm in vacuum (55 mm with chamber top removed)

components.name: Square pinhole (scatter guard) after the KB mirrors
components.distanceNote: Approximate: 'a square pinhole after the KB mirrors' (MEDSI'25); exact position not published. Drawn ~5 mm past the downstream end of the KBH (219.939 m), inside the UHV optics chamber, whose wall sits just upstream of the 47 mm in-vacuum sample space (MEDSI'20).
components.text: A tiny square opening just after the mirrors. It blocks unfocused light and any beam that has bounced off only one of the two mirrors, so only the fully focused beam reaches the sample. Its exact position is not published.

components.name: In-line vacuum optical microscope (XEOL / alignment)
components.distanceNote: Approximate: 'just upstream of the sample' (MEDSI'25).
components.text: A built-in light microscope that looks along the X-ray beam through a small fold mirror with a hole for the X-rays. Users see exactly where the beam lands on the sample, over a 600 µm field with 1 µm resolution, and can send any visible or infrared light the sample gives off (430–1,800 nm) to a spectrometer.

components.name: Sample scanning stack and metrology (ISN instrument 19ID-BI-1)
components.distanceNote: Exact nominal focus: FDR Table 4.49, MEDSI'25. Design geometry gives ~220.4 m.
components.text: The sample rides on a stack of ultra-precise motors that sweep it through the focused beam on the fly, at up to 1 mm/s over a 10 mm range with up to 2 kg on board, plus a rotation stage for 3D. Fifteen laser-interferometer beams measure the sample against the mirrors through frames of Invar and Zerodur, materials that barely expand with heat, so spot and sample can be held together to within the required 4 nm rms (root-mean-square). The sample chamber, separated from the mirrors' ultra-high vacuum by diamond windows and a 2 mm helium gap, can run in vacuum, air or inert gas.

specs.stages: Aerotech PRO225SL and ANT130L; APS vertical flexure stage

components.name: In situ sample environments
components.distanceNote: At the sample position.
components.text: Swap-in mini-laboratories that let the sample work while it is imaged: a liquid-flow cell for batteries and electrochemistry (above 100 °C, with bulk electrodes), a gas cell that heats to 1,000 °C with four electrical bias channels for catalysts, and an APS-built cryostat holder that cools to 40 K (−233 °C), still in development. All three rotate for tomography. The 2017 plan had aimed for 10 K; the as-built cryostat holder starts at 40 K.

specs.media: vacuum, air, inert gas, flowing gas/liquid

components.name: Fluorescence detectors: 7-element SDD and 12-element backscatter SDD
components.distanceNote: At the sample (side/backscatter ports).
components.text: Silicon-drift detectors that sort the X-rays the sample gives off by energy. Every element fluoresces at its own characteristic energies, so each point of the scan reveals which elements are present, even in trace amounts. ISN can use a 7-element detector or a 12-element backscatter detector, both read out by fast Xspress3 Mk2 electronics.

components.name: XBIC/XBIV electrometer
components.distanceNote: At the sample (electrical feedthroughs).
components.text: A very sensitive four-channel current meter (a picoammeter) wired to the sample. In a solar cell or LED it measures the current or voltage that the X-ray spot sets free, point by point, mapping which regions collect charge well.

components.name: Diffraction detector on robot arm (Eiger2 X 1M)
components.distanceNote: Approximate: robot-positioned around and above the sample (MEDSI'25 Fig. 3); variable.
components.text: A diffraction camera carried by an industrial robot arm that steers it around the sample in angle and distance. It catches X-rays diffracted by crystals at telltale angles, through a 0.5 mm beryllium dome window tipped 10° up and 25° outboard (away from the ring), revealing which crystal phases form as the sample is heated or charged.

components.name: Forward ptychography / SAXS detector on 6 m table (Eiger2 X 1M)
components.distanceNote: Approximate: on a downstream XYZ table with 6 m travel along the beam (≈220.5–226.5 m); midpoint shown.
components.text: A camera straight downstream that records the diffraction pattern from each overlapping spot position. A computer works backward from thousands of patterns to an image of a thin sample designed to be sharper than 10 nm, finer than the beam itself. The detector rides a table with 6 m of travel along the beam and also records small-angle scattering and absorption; planning assumed about 3,000 frames a second on average and 5 GB/s of data.

components.name: Mono beamstop (19ID-BS-1)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.49; drawn on the downstream wall of the concrete hutch (NIMA 2020 Fig. 3b).
components.text: The end of the line: a block on the concrete hutch's back wall that safely absorbs whatever is left of the monochromatic beam, 227 m from where it was made.

enclosures.name: Storage-ring tunnel / front end
enclosures.role: accelerator tunnel housing the undulators (straight section) and HHL front end
enclosures.notes: Source point = center of the ID straight. The FOE upstream wall is ~24 m, scaled from the NIMA 2020 plan; the FE exit mask is at 25.4 m inside the FOE.

enclosures.name: 19-ID-A
enclosures.role: first optics enclosure (white/pink beam): M1+M2 tank, DCM, DMM, M3
enclosures.notes: Approx from NIMA 2020 Fig. 2 scaled to FDR distances (~64 px/m at 400 dpi). The end wall matches the 35.8 m start of transport ST-1. Trapezoidal footprint, roughly 1.9–2.4 m wide inside and wider downstream. The PDR planned to reuse the SBC-era 19-ID-A/B as the FOE.

enclosures.name: 19-ID-C
enclosures.role: aperture hutch 1 (monochromatic): PM-3, BC-2, vertical BDA at 55 m
enclosures.notes: Start exact (end of ST-1 per FDR). End approx from the NIMA 2020 plan (wall shared with D). Width ~3.2–4.0 m (tapered). The FDR component table calls the upstream end '19-ID-B'; the 2020 plan labels this room 19-ID-C. The FDR optics text itself puts BDA-V in 'enclosure C' and BDA-H in 'enclosure D'.

enclosures.name: 19-ID-D
enclosures.role: aperture hutch 2: horizontal BDA at 64 m, photon shutter at 65 m
enclosures.notes: Approx from the NIMA 2020 plan (scaled). The long transport starts at 65.5 m (FDR), so the downstream wall is at ~66 m.

enclosures.name: Long transport corridor
enclosures.role: shielded 4-inch vacuum transport across the experiment hall, through the lab/office (LOM) area and an enclosed corridor to the Long Beamline Building
enclosures.notes: FDR 4-1.2: two long corridors connect the LBB to the APS building and the transports pass through some LOM labs and offices. FDR Fig. 4.1 notes lab reconfiguration for sectors 21 and 22. Ion-pump mini-enclosures at 95, 124, 153 and 183 m.

enclosures.name: 19-ID-E
enclosures.role: experimental station: concrete, temperature-stabilized, vibration-isolated endstation in the Long Beamline Building
enclosures.notes: Internal 14.6 m × 6.6 m with roof ~2.8 m above the beam (NIMA 2020). Start/end estimated from window (213.0) and beamstop (227.0). Walls are 12 in (0.3 m) concrete per MEDSI'20/'25 (the 2020 shielding model assumed 20 cm). Instrument slab is 1 m (3 ft 3 in) thick with 0.5 in isolation joints. Adjacent rooms: ISN control area, air lock/vestibule, sample-prep area, wet lab, data closet (MEDSI'25 Fig. 2a). The FDR calls the satellite building 'building 444' (FDR 4-7.7.3).

enclosures.name: 19-ID-E control & support rooms
enclosures.role: user support rooms: ISN control area, airlock, sample-prep area, wet lab and data closets
enclosures.notes: Room list from MEDSI'25 Fig. 2a. They sit on the inboard side of the endstation (FDR Fig. 4.48 plan); the extent drawn here is read from the Long Beamline Building footprint in site.json and is approximate (±1 m).

instruments.name: ISN nanoprobe instrument (19ID-BI-1)
instruments.text: A scanning X-ray microscope on a granite table that floats on air for coarse alignment and locks solid when the air is released. The Kirkpatrick–Baez focusing mirrors sit in their own clean, ultra-high-vacuum box on piezo-driven flexure stages and focus the beam to a spot designed to be about 20 nm wide, some 6 cm beyond the last mirror, inside a separate sample chamber. That chamber can be pumped, filled with gas or opened to air while the mirrors stay untouched; diamond windows and a 2 mm helium gap join the two. Both chambers share an Invar baseplate, and a 15-channel interferometer measures the optics against the sample. Fluorescence, diffraction, ptychography, beam-induced current and luminescence can be combined in the same scan.
detectors: Dectris Eiger2 X 1M on Stäubli TX2-160L robot (XRD/WAXS)
Dectris Eiger2 X 1M on 6 m-travel table (ptychography/SAXS)
sampleEnvironments: High vacuum, air or inert-gas backfill
Hummingbird electrochemical liquid-flow holder (>100 °C, bulk electrodes)
APS closed-cycle He cryostat holder, 40–355 K (in development)

geometryNotes:
Two in-line, not canted, revolver undulators share the 19-ID straight, so the beamline sits on the straight-section axis. The HHL front end is windowless.

Inside 19-ID-A, the beam drops in a vertical dogleg. M1 (28.0 m) reflects down by 5 mrad and M2 (29.0 m) reflects up by 5 mrad. The beam comes out horizontal again but about 5 mm lower (5 mrad × 1.0 m, estimate). PM-1 at 29.7 m stops the undeflected white beam.

The DCM (31.7 m) and DMM (32.7 m) are horizontally deflecting, inboard, small-offset and fixed-exit. They displace the beam sideways but do not change its direction; the offset value is not published. M3 (35.0 m) then deflects 5 mrad inboard. Everything downstream runs on a line rotated 5 mrad inboard of the source axis, which puts the endstation ~0.9 m inboard of the straight-through line at 220 m (185 m × 5 mrad, estimate, before the mono offset).

19-ID-A is the FOE (~23.9–35.8 m), a narrow trapezoid widening downstream. A 12.4 m shielded pipe crosses open floor to 19-ID-C (48.2–~59 m, BDA-V at 55 m). 19-ID-D shares a wall with C (~59–66 m, BDA-H at 64 m, shutter at 65 m). These three are on the experiment-hall floor in the usual APS position outboard of the ring tunnel.

From 65.5 to 213 m the 4-inch pipe continues in a straight line. It leaves the experiment floor, crosses the lab/office module (LOM) area that serves sectors 21–22, and runs in an enclosed corridor to the Long Beamline Building (LBB) outside the ring building. Shielded ion-pump stations sit at 95, 124, 153 and 183 m, i.e. every ~29 m (FDR); the 2018 vacuum model also had smaller pumps at each end of the 146 m pipe. The exact point where it leaves the building is not published; FDR Figs. 4.1 and 4.48 are schematic.

The LBB (building 444 in the FDR; ~24,000 sq ft) is shared with HEXM (20-ID); the same project built the Activated Materials Laboratory next to HEXM. The two long beamlines come from adjacent sectors, so their transports diverge by ~9° (360°/40 sectors); ISN is the lower one in the FDR plan, HEXM the upper.

Endstation 19-ID-E is a concrete hutch, 14.6 × 6.6 m inside, with 12 in walls and roof ~2.8 m above the beam. It sits on a separate 1 m isolated slab, with the control area, airlock, sample-prep area and wet lab alongside. Inside, along the beam: window, filters, beam-conditioning granite blocks, fast shutter, then the UHV KB chamber on a granite table. The focus is 61 mm past the KBH end. Then come the separate sample chamber with a robot-mounted XRD detector above and outboard (Be dome tipped 10° up and 25° outboard), the green 6 m ptychography detector table, and the beamstop on the downstream wall.

KBV reflects upward in the MEDSI'25 drawing, raising the focus ~2 mm above the incoming beam; the FDR schematic draws a downward-facing mirror. KBH deflects horizontally by 5 mrad, direction not published.

For scale, everything from 24 m to 66 m is about 42 m of floor; the next 147 m is just pipe.

interactiveIdeas.title: The pinhole trade-off: buying coherence with photons
interactiveIdeas.concept: Visitors drive two slits (BDA-V at 55 m, BDA-H at 64 m) with sliders and an energy dial (5-30 keV). A live panel shows the beam on each slit (a secondary-source blob ≈6.5 µm tall and ≈28 µm wide FWHM for the as-built M3 position; the 2017 PDR, with the horizontal mirror at 43 m, had ~4-7 µm by ~16-18 µm), the fraction of light that passes, the coherence of the light reaching the 1 mm-wide KB mirror, and the resulting focal spot and flux. Closing the slits sharpens the spot until it hits the diffraction limit, then only costs photons.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Why nanoprobes deliberately throw away most of the beam, why the 'secondary source' makes the focus immune to wobbling upstream optics, and why the brighter, smaller APS-U source means much less is thrown away.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Coherence-matched aperture: Δ ≈ 0.44 λ z / A, with A = L·sinθ (KB acceptance). V: z ≈ 165 m, A ≈ 404 mm × 2.5 mrad ≈ 1.01 mm → Δ_V ≈ 3.6 µm at 25 keV, 8.9 µm at 10 keV. H: z ≈ 155.9 m, A ≈ 0.32 mm → Δ_H ≈ 10.5 µm at 25 keV, 26 µm at 10 keV. FDR minimum aperture is ~3.5-4 µm. Demagnification: 1/417 (V), 1/1242 (H), so a 4 µm slit images to ~10 nm (V) and a 13 µm slit to ~10 nm (H). Spot ≈ quadrature sum of the slit image and the diffraction limit (plus figure-error blur). Opening past the secondary-source size adds no flux. Geometric estimate for the flat-beam source (σx 14.5 µm, σy 3.1 µm): V ≈ 7.2 µm × 26/29 ≈ 6.5 µm FWHM; H ≈ 34 µm × 29/35 ≈ 28 µm FWHM with M3 at 35 m (PDR: 4.4-6.6 µm V, 16-18 µm H with the mirror at 43 m). Round-beam mode makes the V blob ~2.7× larger. FDR anchors: coherent 16 × 16 nm at 3.4 × 10¹¹ ph/s vs open 24 × 30 nm at 3.1 × 10¹² ph/s (25 keV).

interactiveIdeas.title: Why 220 metres? Spot size vs working distance
interactiveIdeas.concept: A side view of the KB mirror pair with draggable mirror length and working distance (5-100 mm), and an energy dial. The display shows the focal spot, the cone angle (NA) and a cartoon in situ cell that either fits in the gap or collides with the mirror. A second panel moves the BDA-to-mirror distance: shorten the beamline and the slit must close to sub-micrometre sizes to keep a long mirror coherently lit, so flux collapses.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: For a given spot size, more working distance needs a longer mirror. A longer mirror needs a wider coherent beam, which needs a longer beamline. That chain is why ISN has its own building.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Diffraction-limited FWHM ≈ 0.88 λ q / (L sinθ) with q = L/2 + W (X. Shi 2016). With L_H = 129 mm, q = 125.5 mm, θ = 2.5 mrad: 17 nm at 25 keV, 42 nm at 10 keV, ~88 nm at 4.8 keV. Spot ∝ λ, so low energies give bigger spots. NA ≈ half the angular spread of rays leaving the mirror ≈ 1.7 mrad. Coherent illumination requires Δ ≤ 0.44 λ z / (L sinθ); for Δ ≈ 3.6 µm at 25 keV, a 1 mm acceptance needs z ≈ 165 m (≈185 m for Δ = 4 µm). Pitfalls: grazing-incidence reflectivity cut-off of Pt at ~2.5 mrad near 30-40 keV; the FDR fixes θ at 2.5 mrad. The 2.5 mrad angle is set by Pt: its critical angle is ≈ 84 mrad·keV / E (estimate from δ), i.e. ≈2.5 mrad near 34 keV, just above the 30 keV top of the range.

interactiveIdeas.title: The nanoradian challenge
interactiveIdeas.concept: A giant lever arm game: visitors tilt a virtual KB mirror with a knob whose smallest step is 1 nrad and watch the 20 nm spot drift across a sample of nanoparticles. Toggle 'heater on' (a 0.01 °C change on a 50 mm steel support) and footsteps in the hall to see what moves the spot, then switch on the real ISN fixes: Invar/Zerodur frames, an isolated 1 m slab, air socks and interferometers.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: How tiny angular errors become nanometre blur, and why the endstation is a building-scale vibration and thermal engineering project.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Spot shift ≈ 2·Δθ·q. KBV: 2 × 5 nrad × 0.396 m ≈ 4 nm (20% of 20 nm); KBH: 2 × 16 nrad × 0.1255 m ≈ 4 nm. These match the stated 5/16 nrad requirements. Measured KBV noise is 0.4 nrad rms, 1.7 nrad p-p. 5 nrad = 5 mm tilt over 1,000 km. Thermal expansion: steel α ≈ 12 × 10⁻⁶/K, so 50 mm × 0.01 K ≈ 6 nm; Invar α ≈ 10⁻⁶/K → ≈0.5 nm. Requirements: air ±0.05 °C/h, surfaces ±0.01 °C/h, VC-G 0.78 µm/s rms (1-100 Hz).

interactiveIdeas.title: One pixel, five answers
interactiveIdeas.concept: A fly-scan animation over a solar-cell cross-section. Click any pixel to open five synchronized readouts: an XRF spectrum (Cu, In, Ga, Se peaks), a diffraction pattern from the robot detector, a ptychography speckle pattern, an XBIC current trace and an XEOL spectrum. Toggling to a 'map' view assembles each channel into an image, and the visitor finds the defect that kills current.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Multimodal correlative imaging: composition, structure, electrical performance and optical emission measured at the same 20 nm spot at the same instant.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Excitation must exceed the absorption edge: Se K-edge 12.66 keV (Kα 11.22), Ga 10.37 (Kα 9.25), Cu 8.98 (Kα 8.05), In K-edge 27.94 keV (Kα 24.2) or L lines ~3.3-3.9 keV. Choose ~13-15 keV for CIGS K-lines without In-K. At 30 keV K-edges are reachable up to Sn (29.2 keV); heavier elements use L lines. Fly-scan timing: 1 mm/s with 20 nm pixels = 50,000 pixels/s (20 µs dwell), but ptychography needs ≥~60% probe overlap, so with a ~20-30 nm probe the step is ≤ ~8-12 nm and a ~3 kHz frame rate limits the scan to ~25-35 µm/s. It also needs a coherent probe (BDAs closed).

interactiveIdeas.title: Through the window: choosing the energy for an in situ cell
interactiveIdeas.concept: Build a cell: pick window material and thickness (Si3N4, diamond, Kapton), electrolyte depth (0-2 mm water) and gas path, then slide the X-ray energy. Bars show the incident beam surviving to the sample and the fluorescence of a chosen element escaping back to the detector. Low energy makes the sample glow brightly but the light can't get out; high energy goes through everything but some elements can no longer be seen in their K lines.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Why ISN uses hard X-rays up to 30 keV plus a large working distance: real environments (liquids, gases, windows) absorb soft X-rays, and both the incoming beam and the outgoing fluorescence must survive.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Beer-Lambert T = exp(-(μ/ρ)ρt). Water μ/ρ ≈ 41.9 cm²/g (5 keV), 5.33 (10 keV), 0.81 (20 keV), 0.38 (30 keV) (NIST XCOM). So 1 mm water transmits ~1.5% at 5 keV, ~59% at 10 keV, ~92% at 20 keV and ~96% at 30 keV; 200 µm transmits ~43% at 5 keV. Fluorescence escape uses the emission-line energy, not the beam energy (e.g., Fe Kα 6.4 keV through 1 mm water: μ/ρ ≈ 20 cm²/g, so ≈13%). ISN chambers use single-crystal diamond windows with a 2 mm He gap, and the XRD Be dome is 0.5 mm.

interactiveIdeas.title: Zoom from millimetres to nanometres (hierarchical imaging)
interactiveIdeas.concept: Start with a 10 mm battery electrode or catalyst pellet mapped coarsely, then zoom 3-4 decades to a single 20 nm-resolved particle. A clock shows how long each zoom level takes at ISN fly-scan speeds versus a pre-upgrade nanoprobe. The 'needle in a haystack' is a rare contaminant particle.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Why fast scanning plus a large field (10 × 10 mm, 2 kg cells) matters: the defects that control performance are rare and must be found before they can be studied.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Scan time ≈ (rows) × (row length / speed) + overheads. A 10 × 10 mm map at 1 µm pixels and 1 mm/s = 10,000 rows × 10 s ≈ 28 h. A 10 × 10 µm map at 20 nm pixels = 500 rows × 10 ms ≈ 5 s of motion, but counting statistics (flux ~10¹¹-10¹² ph/s) and detector rates set the real dwell. Stage limits: 1 mm/s horizontal; vertical 1 mm/s only for ROI <90 µm, otherwise 0.1 mm/s. Data volume: ~10 PB/yr planned.

funFacts: ISN is the longest beamline at the APS. Argonne describes it as sitting 720 feet from the storage ring. The instrument is 220 m from the undulator source and the beamstop is at 227 m.
The Long Beamline Building's beamlines are about three times longer than other APS beamlines, roughly two football fields.

ISN predates the MBA upgrade: a 2013 concept already described it. In the 2015 Early Science report the MBA-era optical design was a 180 m beamline. It grew to 220 m so long focusing mirrors could be lit with coherent light while keeping a 5–6 cm working distance, and the 2017 PDR says the final length was chosen so ISN and HEXM could share one satellite building.

During commissioning the vertical focusing mirror held its angle to 0.4 nanoradians rms, measured in air with the vacuum pumps off. That is like tilting a 1,000 km plank by 0.4 mm at the far end (the analogy is simple arithmetic).
The endstation air is held to ±0.05 °C for an hour and the instrument surfaces to ±0.01 °C. Fabric 'air socks' blow gentle laminar air, and the exhaust fan is kept outside the room.
The microscope room stands on its own 1-metre-thick concrete slab, cut free from the rest of the building by isolation joints, to meet the VC-G vibration criterion of 0.78 µm/s.

The two tiny beam-defining slits can be hit by up to ~11.6 W of focused X-rays when the multilayer monochromator is used (0.2 W with the crystal monochromator). A slit facing the beam head-on would heat past 850 K and be destroyed, so the jaws are designed to take the beam at a grazing angle.
The 404 mm vertical focusing mirror is about 20 million times longer than the spot it makes.
ISN was expected to generate ~10 petabytes of raw data a year, nearly 15× what the APS's 2-ID-D ptychography, 2-ID-E XRF and Bio-Nanoprobe instruments produced together (~730 TB).

Before ISN, 19-ID was the Structural Biology Center's protein-crystallography undulator beamline: 2,277 publications came from 19-ID. SBC planned to support users until the APS 'dark' period began in April 2023. It has since concluded operations and handed over to the multi-beamline eBERlight program.

U.S. Energy Secretary Jennifer Granholm cut the ribbon on the Long Beamline Building on 25 July 2022. Argonne held a ceremonial groundbreaking on 23 July 2020, with construction scheduled to start that fall; Argonne's 2022 release says ground was broken in June 2020.

The first ISN concept (2013–14, before the MBA upgrade) planned KB mirrors for a 50 nm high-flux spot and zone plates or multilayer Laue lenses for 20 nm. The upgraded source and a 220 m beamline let the final design reach ~20 nm with mirrors alone, keeping a long working distance.
Samples can be cycled from 40 K (−233 °C) to more than 1,000 °C, in vacuum, air or flowing gas, while being scanned at up to 1 mm/s.

openQuestions: Final focal spot. Design is 20 × 20 nm FWHM at 25 keV (FDR, directory). The MRS Fall 2025 and XRM 2026 abstracts state 25–30 nm at 25 keV, and MEDSI'25 says preliminary measurements 'show promise' of 20 nm. No published measured spot or flux at the sample yet.

DMM status. The FDR specifies a Mo/B₄C double-multilayer monochromator (19ID-MN-2), and the 2020 FOE drawing shows it. The 2026 Beamline Directory lists only an 'LN₂-cooled H-DCM'. It is unclear whether the DMM was installed or commissioned.

Working distance has four published values: 61 mm (optical, MEDSI'20/'25); 60 mm nominal and 55 mm with the KB enclosure (FDR, feature page, 2025–26 abstracts); 47 mm usable in vacuum (MEDSI'20); and '20–50 mm depending on configuration' (Directory). The distance is about 55–61 mm optically, and less in practice once chambers and detectors are in place.

M3 position. The FDR component table and the 2020 FOE drawing place M3 at 35.0 m inside 19-ID-A. FDR Fig. 4.40 and the 2017 PDR show the horizontal focusing mirror at 43 m. 35 m is taken here as the as-built position.
FE exit mask: 2 × 2 mm² (FDR ch. 3 and 4) vs 2 (H) × 1 (V) mm (Sunil 2020 shielding study). As-built value unconfirmed.

Enclosure naming and boundaries. The FDR component table refers to transport 'from 19-ID-A to 19-ID-B', but the 2020 shielding plan shows only A, C, D and E; the PDR planned to reuse SBC-era A/B as the FOE. Hutch extents here are scaled from a 2020 drawing (±0.5 m), not an as-built survey.

Instrument distance: 220 m in the FDR, PDR, SPIE 2021, MEDSI'25 and Directory, versus 210 m in MEDSI'20 and 250 m (820 ft) in Argonne's July 2020 groundbreaking release and a contractor page. 220 m is adopted. The as-built KB numbers (p = 165.004 m, q = 396 mm) put the focus at 220.4 m if BDA-V is at exactly 55.0 m, or BDA-V at 54.6 m if the focus is at 220.0 m.

Undulator description. FDR ch. 4 says 'a revolver undulator of 4.6 m length'; FDR ch. 3 and the 2026 ID table show two in-line ~2.35 m revolvers (U21/U25 each). Whether an active phase shifter is installed between them at 19-ID is not confirmed publicly.

SPIE 2021 abstract quotes coherent flux 'above 4 × 10¹² ph/s at 5 keV, and 6 × 10¹² ph/s at 30 keV'. That is inconsistent with FDR Table 4.51 (4.7 × 10¹¹ ph/s at 25 keV after the BDAs) and may be a transcription error. FDR values are used here.
KB reflection directions. MEDSI'25 Fig. 5a shows KBV reflecting upward; FDR Fig. 4.50 draws it facing down. KBH inboard/outboard direction is not published. DCM/DMM lateral offset is not published.

Operating mode. Flat-beam vs round-beam storage-ring mode changes the vertical source size (3.1 vs 8.3 µm rms) and so the BDA-V settings and coherent flux. Which mode is standard for 2026 user runs was not confirmed here.
Endstation wall thickness: 12 in concrete (MEDSI'20, MEDSI'25 Fig. 2b) vs 20 cm assumed in the 2020 shielding model. 12 in is taken as as-built.

Status nuance. The Directory says 'Operational/Accepting General Users' (Oct 2026), but a July 2026 job posting still cites commissioning. The scope of the general-user program (techniques and environments offered) is not documented publicly.

Horizontal secondary-source size. With M3 at 35 m (as built) the 64 m BDA-H sees the source at ~0.83×, about 28 µm FWHM in flat-beam mode (estimate), not the ~16–18 µm quoted in the 2017 PDR for a mirror at 43 m. The FDR's '~11 km' M3 radius also matches the 43 m layout. Measured BDA-plane beam sizes are not published.
Construction start of the LBB: ceremonial groundbreaking 23 Jul 2020 with construction 'scheduled to begin this fall' versus 'broke ground for construction in June 2020' in the 2022 release.
As-built KB figure-error spec '<2.0 nm' (MEDSI'25 Fig. 5a) does not state rms or peak-to-valley; the FDR rms targets were 0.38/0.45 nm. Coating (FDR: Pt) is not restated in the as-built paper.
